  "text": "## Cost-Effectiveness of Cerebrolysin after Ischemic Stroke: Secondary Analysis of the CARS Study

## Abstract
The cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin as an add-on therapy for moderate–severe acute ischemic stroke is a topic that remains understudied. This study aims to address this gap by performing a comprehensive cost-utility analysis using both deterministic and probabilistic methods from a payer perspective and within the Romanian inpatient care setting. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were calculated using partial individual patient data from the 2016 Cerebrolysin and Recovery After Stroke (CARS) trial, utilizing three different health state valuation models. Cost data was extracted from actual acute care costs reported by Romanian public hospitals for reimbursement purposes for patients included in the CARS study. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were calculated for each treatment arm for the duration of the clinical trial. Deterministic analysis based on sample mean values indicates Cerebrolysin would be cost-effective at a threshold between roughly 18.8 and 29.9 thousand EUR, depending on valuation techniques. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis results indicate an 80% chance probability of cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin as an add-on therapy for acute ischemic stroke, considering a willingness-to-pay threshold of 50,000 EUR in a 90-day timeframe after stroke. Further economic evaluations of Cerebrolysin are needed to strengthen these findings, covering a timeframe of at least 12 months after the acute incident, which would account for treatment effects spanning beyond the first 90 days after ischemic stroke. These should be conducted to determine its cost-effectiveness under various care settings and patient pathways. Most importantly, modelling techniques are needed to answer important questions such as the estimates of population gain in QALYs after acute administration of Cerebrolysin and the potential offsetting of direct medical costs as a result of administering the intervention.

## 1. Introduction
Stroke continues to be one of the leading death and disability causes worldwide, with 12.2 million new cases (among which 62.4% were ischemic) and 6.55 million deaths in 2019 [[1]]. A major public health issue, the stroke is projected to hold its global rank by 2040 on the list of causes for years of life lost [[2]]. Acute management of stroke has progressed significantly in the past decades, resulting in a considerable reduction in mortality rates [[3]], while advances in neurorehabilitation have led to improvement in outcomes after stroke [[4]]. To alleviate the global burden of stroke, continuous expansion of care networks, improvements in care standards and proper implementation of primary and secondary prevention guidelines are required [[5],[6]]. The changing age distribution of populations and increasing economic burden of innovation with health technologies have powerful implications for both the supply and demand of healthcare services [[7],[8]]. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused major disturbances in this already fragile equilibrium by redirecting resources and redesigning health services delivery priority [[9],[10]], generating a tsunami of unforeseen health care needs for both communicable and non-communicable diseases and creating consequential setbacks in most other disease areas [[11]]. An increasing body of evidence points out that stroke admissions have substantially decreased during the pandemic [[12],[13],[14],[15]] and measured time of stroke care acute indicators (door-to-imaging, door-to-needle, door-to-groin, door-to-reperfusion) for assisted cases have increased [[16]].

The ability of countries to simultaneously navigate crises and tackle long-term challenges is largely dependent on socioeconomic context [[17]], as impoverished health systems are less equipped to focus on the shifting health needs of the population [[18]]. In the context of low health expenditure, circumstantial resource allocation and poor mechanisms for health technology assessment often considerably hinder improvement in populational health. As a result of this constellation of determinants, health systems are under unprecedented distress, while being forced to operate under budgetary constraints similar to the pre-pandemic period. The importance of developing and incorporating cost-effectiveness evidence in health decision making and resource allocation is becoming paramount, even as the world prepares to return to “normal” once COVID-19 reaches an endemic phase [[17]].

The landscape of stroke care is rapidly evolving, and the incorporation of novel therapeutic approaches and technologies is essential to improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. With an aging population and an increase in the prevalence of risk factors, such as hypertension, obesity and diabetes, the demand for efficient and cost-effective stroke treatments will continue to rise [[1]]. In addition, the complexity and interrelated nature of stroke pathophysiology and treatment necessitates a multidisciplinary approach, which can prove challenging in the context of constrained resources and competing healthcare priorities [[19]].

As healthcare systems worldwide strive to optimize the allocation of resources and improve patient outcomes, cost-effectiveness analysis plays a crucial role in informing policy decisions and clinical practice guidelines [[20]]. The integration of economic evaluations into the decision-making process can help identify the most efficient use of limited healthcare resources and facilitate the adoption of new therapies that provide the greatest value to patients and society [[21]]. Given the significant human and economic impact of a stroke, the assessment of cost-effectiveness for emerging therapies is of particular importance to ensure that healthcare systems can provide optimal care while maintaining financial sustainability [[22]].

Cerebrolysin is a promising biological agent that mimics the biological action of neurotrophic factors, aiding both neuroprotection and neurorecovery after ischemic stroke. It has been recently included in several clinical guidelines [[23],[24],[25]] and is particularly recommended as an add-on treatment in moderate–severe cases. Cerebrolysin is a peptide-based medication derived from porcine brain tissue, which contains a mixture of neurotrophic factors and active peptides that demonstrate neuroprotective and neurorestorative properties. The mechanism of action of Cerebrolysin is multifaceted, involving reduced inflammation, decreased apoptosis, enhanced neurogenesis and increased synaptic plasticity [[26]]. These combined effects contribute to the improvement of neurological outcomes and functional recovery in patients with ischemic stroke. Several clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy and safety of Cerebrolysin as an adjunct therapy to standard stroke care, with better functional outcomes and lower rates of adverse events compared to placebo [[27],[28]]. Cerebrolysin has shown potential benefits in other neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer’s disease and traumatic brain injury [[29],[30],[31]]. Although it is emerging as part of care standards, there is little evidence regarding the cost-effectiveness profile of Cerebrolysin [[32],[33]].

Our research seeks to expand current knowledge on this topic by providing a new cost-utility assessment on Cerebrolysin as complementary treatment for moderate to severe ischemic stroke. Understanding the agent’s cost-effectiveness profile is critical to inform decision-makers and clinicians of the potential value it could provide in the management of ischemic stroke. As healthcare systems grapple with the challenges of delivering high-quality care under budgetary constraints, the generation of robust cost-effectiveness evidence for Cerebrolysin can help support its integration into clinical practice and optimize the use of limited resources.

Moreover, the examination of cost-effectiveness in the context of the Romanian healthcare system is particularly relevant, given its unique challenges and the need for evidence-based decision-making. Romania faces considerable disparities in access to healthcare services, particularly in rural areas, and is characterized by a high degree of fragmentation in service provision [[34]]. In addition, the country has one of the lowest healthcare expenditures in the European Union, resulting in a significant unmet need for quality care [[35]]. By conducting a cost-utility analysis of Cerebrolysin within the Romanian inpatient care setting, this study aims to provide valuable insights for policymakers and healthcare providers in addressing the specific needs and constraints of the local context. Furthermore, the secondary analysis of the CARS study offers a unique opportunity to assess the cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin using real-world data from a well-designed clinical trial. By leveraging individual patient data and actual acute care costs reported by Romanian public hospitals, the findings of this study can help bridge the gap between clinical efficacy and the economic implications of Cerebrolysin as an add-on therapy for moderate–severe acute ischemic stroke.

This study seeks to provide a comprehensive assessment of the cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin in the context of the Romanian healthcare system, contributing to the evidence base for its potential value in improving stroke outcomes and informing healthcare decision-making. By combining clinical, economic and policy perspectives, our research aims to shed light on the complex interplay between stroke care, resource allocation and health outcomes, ultimately providing valuable insights for the ongoing development and refinement of stroke management strategies.

## 2. Materials and Methods
Using deterministic and probabilistic approaches, we conducted a cost-utility evaluation to compute the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for Cerebrolysin, drawing on information gathered from multiple sources. Deterministic methods (using fixed input values) in economic evaluations involve calculating cost-effectiveness using single-point estimates for all input parameters, such as costs, effectiveness and utilities. This approach does not account for uncertainty or variability in the input parameters, and thus, the results may not reflect the full range of possible outcomes. Probabilistic methods (incorporating uncertainty) in economic evaluations, on the other hand, use probability distributions for input parameters to account for uncertainty and variability. By performing multiple simulations, these methods generate a range of possible outcomes, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the cost-effectiveness and the likelihood of different scenarios occurring. Due to the nature of data collection (secondary analysis of clinical trial data; extraction of anonymized and aggregated cost values for various care scenarios), Institutional Review Board approval was not required for this study. To simulate patient pathways and costs, we selected the main care setting from the only available clinical trial that may be used to derive utilities for inpatient acute ischemic stroke care, based on the dominant participating country (Romania). This analysis was performed from the perspective of the payer, based on a predefined sequence (Figure 1).

## 2.1. Deriving Utilities for the Intervention and Standard of Care
We obtained individual patient data from the 2016 Cerebrolysin and Recovery After Stroke (CARS) trial from the principal investigators [[36]]. Patient demographics, medical history, risk factors and 36-Item-Short-Form-Survey (SF-36) results (n = 208) were transferred to a Microsoft Excel workbook and further processed and analyzed to assess baseline comparability and to obtain individual patient utilities for Cerebrolysin in the parallel quasi-experimental paradigm. SF-36 data consisted of single score values at day 2 and day 90 after stroke onset (visit 2 and visit 7, respectively). The resulting database included 198 patients. SF-36 values were converted to health utility scores using converters [[37]] developed by School of Health and Related Research (ScHARR) at the University of Sheffield. Several instances of missing SF-36 data were handled by excluding cases with missing values on more than 3 SF-36 subscales on either visit (n = 10) or by recoding missing entries as 9 (n = 13), according to the instructions of the SF-36 to SF-6D utility score converter. The tool generated three different types of utility scores using standard gamble, ordinal and Bayesian posterior mean health state valuation models. Due to missing values, the converter excluded an additional 5 cases, resulting in 193 patients included in the final analysis (100—Cerebrolysin; 93—placebo).

The utility scores generated were used to calculate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) for the first year after stroke onset. Three values were obtained for each patient based on the health state valuation models used in the convertor tool. The formula used to calculate QALYs for each individual patient was:2 ∗ D 2 + 88 ∗ A V E R A G E D 2 , D 90 / 90 ∗ 0.25 where D2 is the utility score for day 2 and D90 is the utility score for day 90. The assumptions within this QALY calculation fit the definitions and timeline for stroke recovery set by Bernhardt et al. (2017), where improvement is registered in the acute and early subacute phases (up to day 90), followed by a plateau in neurorecovery [[38]].

## 2.2. Extracting Costs with Acute Ischemic Stroke
Cost data on inpatient standard treatment of stroke was determined by analyzing actual costs from the acute hospitalization of the CARS study. Reported sums include direct (staff wages, medication, supplies, diagnostic services) and indirect (administration and overhead) hospital costs associated with inpatient care. Costs were converted from RON to EUR based on an average conversion rate between 15 November and 15 December 2021 of 1 EUR = 4.95 RON and rounded to the nearest integer value. The cost for one therapeutic unit (10 mL) of Cerebrolysin was retrieved from the webpage of the Romanian National Health Insurance House (5.5 EUR per 10 mL vial). This cost represents the maximal price set by national legislation and covers the most expensive scenario. Given that the treatment course used in the CARS study consisted of 30 mL of Cerebrolysin per day, diluted with physiological saline solution to a total volume of 100 mL, we added the cost of a 100 mL vial of saline solution (0.6 EUR) to the cost of three Cerebrolysin 10 mL vials. The price for a 100 mL saline solution vial was worked out by gathering the prices for 20 vial boxes from 3 independent sources (the websites of major distributors of pharmaceutical products in Romania) and averaging the per-vial price. The resulting price describes the theoretical daily cost of the Cerebrolysin add-on therapy from the CARS study to the standard treatment of ischemic stroke. Costs were then converted across currencies based on the referenced conversion rate and rounded to the nearest single decimal value. Costs for acute discharges below 21 days were estimated at 150 RON (30 EUR) per day for infusion. An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to acute care costs.

## 2.3. Calculating the Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio of Cerebrolysin Add-on Therapy for Ischemic Stroke Using a Deterministic Approach
Having computed the costs described above, we calculated the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for the Cerebrolysin add-on therapy compared to the standard treatment of ischemic stroke from the CARS study: 30 mL per day, diluted in physiological saline solution up to a total of 100 mL, for 21 days. The formula used for calculating the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios in all scenarios was:c o s t o f a d d e d C e r e b r o l y s i n A - c o s t o f s t a n d a r d t r e a t m e n t B Q A L Y s C e r e b r o l y s i n C - Q A L Y s p l a c e b o D

We calculated three ICER values, one for each of the three different health state valuation models used for generating health utilities based on which QALYs were calculated.

## 2.4. Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis
Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) was performed to deal with parameter uncertainty and the hypothetical nature of the scenarios and inputs used for deterministic ICER calculations. We used a custom MS Excel spreadsheet to perform 10,000 ICER simulations per patient pathway and represented these on cost-effectiveness planes. Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) were constructed by plotting probabilities for the cost-effectiveness of the intervention against threshold increments up to 50,000 EUR. PSA random sampling was performed based on log normal (QALYs) or uniform (costs) distributions. The highest and lowest aggregate values by health state valuation model were used as the upper and lower bounds of QALY distributions for patient groups.

## 3. Results
We compared baseline characteristics (demographics, stroke severity, social and medical history) of the 193 patients for whom we calculated QALYs. No major differences were found, allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups.

The QALYs calculated using the utilities resulting from SF-36 to SF-6D conversion were aggregated by health state valuation model: standard gamble (0.698 Cerebrolysin vs. 0.643 placebo), ordinal (0.704 Cerebrolysin vs. 0.647 placebo) and Bayesian posterior mean (0.653 Cerebrolysin vs. 0.613 placebo). Average total costs per patient were 7214 RON (1458 EUR) for Cerebrolysin and 5197 RON (1050 EUR) for placebo. This amounts to a mean increment in treatment cost difference between patients treated with Cerebrolysin and standard care of 2017 RON (408 EUR), as highlighted in Table 1, and a mean increment in QALYs between 0.01–0.015, depending on the valuation technique (Table 2).

Three different ICER values corresponding to the health state valuation models used are presented in Table 2. The lowest ICER values were determined based on the ordinal valuation (18,788 EUR/QALY), while the highest were concluded for the Bayesian posterior valuation method (26,981 EUR/QALY).

## Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis
Based on the CARS trial patient pathway, the Cerebrolysin add-on treatment was cost-effective in roughly 80% of cases for an ICER threshold set at 50,000 EUR (Figure 2 and Figure 3), considering only the 90-day timeframe of the CARS-study.

## 4. Discussion
In this study, we aimed to appraise the cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin add-on therapy compared to standard care for acute ischemic stroke by calculating ICER values for different cost scenarios using deterministic and probabilistic methods. Assuming that Cerebrolysin add-on therapy generates no additional costs with extra hospitalization, we concluded the agent to be cost-effective 80% of the time considering a high willingness-to-pay threshold. Our findings are in line with the scarce existing literature on this topic [[32],[33]], providing much-needed additional evidence of the economic viability of this therapy. The next step would be to conduct a budget impact analysis that would accompany the results produced by our study [[39]].

Kulikov and Abdrashitova have conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of Cerebrolysin in moderate and severe patients and have reported life years gained (LYG) as an efficiency criterion. Their inquiry demonstrated that Cerebrolysin (vs. standard stroke therapy) is a dominant intervention. The CER (cost-effectiveness ratio) for Cerebrolysin was 2367 EUR less compared to standard stroke therapy [[32]]. Walter et al. [[33]] employed a Markov-model on a horizon of 10 years from the payer’s perspective and used mRS data collected (from multiple sources) at day 90 post-stroke and reported health benefits in terms of QALYs and life years (LYs). This study demonstrated that Cerebrolysin is cost-effective as it reduces costs incurred in acute care and nursing homes. However, the difference between Cerebrolysin and rt-PA vs. rt-PA are slightly higher for the first scenario (3.77 vs. 3.75 QALYs).

Additionally, our examination includes the CARS treatment methodology, which involves an extended duration of hospitalization to conclude the 21-day Cerebrolysin regimen. These circumstances apply to healthcare environments where the guidance from expert organizations to establish comprehensive physical rehabilitation initiatives following an ischemic stroke [[40],[41]] is adhered to. Within this framework, we have found that Cerebrolysin proves to be cost-effective in 80% of cases when considering a higher willingness-to-pay limit. Conversely, a lower threshold renders the intervention less financially viable, indicating that providing Cerebrolysin in an outpatient setting after prompt discharge would serve as a suitable alternative to prolonging hospital stays solely for Cerebrolysin administration, which would impose an unwarranted fiscal burden on healthcare budgets.

To our knowledge, this study yields the first explicit measure of change in QALY values between standard therapy and Cerebrolysin add-on scheme for ischemic stroke in the first year after the event. Aggregated QALYs for the Cerebrolysin group were higher than those for the placebo group (0.051 average difference across the three health state valuation models), indicating that the Cerebrolysin add-on scheme has a beneficial impact on quality of life of ischemic stroke patients. The SF-36 to utility converter from the University of Sheffield provides three options for generating health utility scores: standard gamble, ordinal and Bayesian posterior mean. Each of these approaches employs a different health state valuation model to transform SF-36 data into utility scores. The standard gamble method is based on the concept of risk preference, wherein individuals are asked to choose between a certain health outcome and a gamble with a probability of either perfect health or a less desirable outcome. This method captures the individual’s preferences and risk tolerance in relation to different health states. The ordinal approach, on the other hand, ranks health states according to their desirability, without considering the magnitude of preference between them. This approach is simpler to implement but may not capture the full spectrum of preference differences between health states. Lastly, the Bayesian posterior mean model combines prior beliefs and observed data to generate health utility scores. This method accounts for uncertainty and can adaptively update utility scores as new data become available. Using all three valuation models and comparing their results can offer valuable insights into the robustness and sensitivity of the derived utility scores. By doing so, we can assert that there are no potential variations in preferences and risk attitudes which may impact the overall cost-effectiveness analysis.

Our findings should be interpreted in conjunction with the selected study setting. The Romanian healthcare system, based on social health insurance, features significant government involvement, with the Ministry of Health (MoH) playing a central role in regulation, control and coordination. Public Health Directorates at the county level implement MoH directives and oversee local healthcare tasks. The MoH also coordinates other governmental healthcare institutions, such as the National Health Insurance House, the National Agency for Medicines and Medical Devices and the National Authority for Quality Management in Health Care. Local public authorities and the Romanian Parliament also influence the healthcare system. In Romania, the healthcare system heavily emphasizes inpatient care, with insufficient focus on primary, ambulatory and preventive care. Access to healthcare remains a challenge, particularly in rural areas, leading to high levels of unmet medical needs. Stroke care in Romania involves many stakeholders, including emergency medicine, intensive care, neurology, neurosurgery, radiology and rehabilitation. The pre-hospital phase is managed by the Ambulance Service and the Mobile Emergency Service for Resuscitation (SMURD). Patients are transported to hospitals with designated stroke acute care units. The rehabilitation process begins in the neurology ward or in a dedicated rehabilitation unit [[42]]. In 2015, the MoH introduced the “Priority Action-Stroke” (PAS) program to finance reperfusion treatment for acute ischemic stroke and endovascular treatment for subarachnoid hemorrhage. Initially covering 10 hospitals, the program expanded to 44 hospitals performing intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) by 2021. However, only a few hospitals can perform endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for stroke patients, while the rest can only conduct intravenous thrombolysis. Notably, most hospitals are not meeting comprehensive stroke unit standards, as defined by the European Stroke Organization (ESO) [[43]]. From 2015 to 2018, around 1800 patients received reperfusion treatment through the PAS program, as reported by the Romanian Ministry of Health. The percentage of patients receiving IVT treatment was 0.8% in 2017. By 2022, 3242 patients received reperfusion treatment, accounting for 7.8% of all ischemic stroke patients. This marks a significant improvement but falls short against the estimate of patients eligible for pharmacological reperfusion and the ESO’s 15% recommended minimum rate for IVT. In 2021, only 0.9% of patients underwent EVT, well below the estimated 10% of eligible patients and the ESO’s 5% target for 2030 [[44]].

Cerebrolysin is reimbursed in Romania in the acute setting and in the open pharmaceutical circuit under list B (50% reimbursement). This means that, currently, there is a combination of uses and protocols within its market authorization of a 10–50 mL daily dosage for ischemic stroke. Therefore, the budget impact of normalizing care in line with the CARS protocol is impossible to measure without a high-quality observational study to assess how and how much Cerebrolysin is currently being used. An opportunity to explore this topic will emerge upon completion of the C-REGS 2 registry study [[45]]. Nevertheless, based on incident strokes reported by the Romanian Society of Neurology in 2022 (n = 37.225), a gross assumption that around 80% of cases would fit the ischemic indication [[46]], and of those, two-thirds of cases would be moderate–severe and hence, eligible for Cerebrolysin treatment, the incremental cost difference from our study (408 EUR) and the estimated budget impact of treating acute stroke patients for 21 days with Cerebrolysin in line with the CARS protocol would be roughly 8.5 million EUR per year, assuming the intervention would not currently exist on the market, which is around 5% of the healthcare economic burden of stroke in the country [[43],[47]]. In addition to this proportionally small estimated budget impact (which we stress is likely overestimated in such gross calculations), given that overall stroke expenditure in Romania is up to tenfold less than other countries in Europe and the current increasing trend of expenditure at the national level [[46],[48]], we assert that the normalization of Cerebrolysin treatment in line with the CARS protocol would entail a manageable budget impact for the Romanian healthcare system.

The limitations of our study predominantly arise from the care setting in which Cerebrolysin outcomes were determined and on which the costing exercise was based. While a 21-day treatment course is more than plausible, the guideline recommendation that Cerebrolysin is administered for a minimum of 10 days [[23]] allows for an assessment of the cost-effectiveness of this agent for shorter treatment courses. Such analyses would further enlighten our perspective on the economic viability of Cerebrolysin and could constitute strong evidence for its wide adoption, even in health systems with less abundant resources. The information surfaced by our study, although building a favorable cost-effectiveness profile for Cerebrolysin, calls for further economic evaluations of this treatment in different care settings along various other patient pathways and exploring issues such as the impact of the intervention on direct medical cost, recurrence and effects beyond the 90-day span of the CARS trial.

These limitations are balanced by the broadness of our methodological approach and set of tools employed. Firstly, health utilities for Cerebrolysin and standard of care have been derived using three different health state valuation models, consequently resulting in three types of ICER values. Cost data was extracted from the same care setting which utilities were derived from, hence, decreasing overall uncertainty. Furthermore, our probability sensitivity analysis accounts for several patient profiles and pathways in this specific care setting. Data from another study assessing cost of inpatient stroke care in the same exact setting [[47]] rendered similar values for daily hospitalization as our costing exercise did. The theoretical cost of the Cerebrolysin treatment course has been built to reflect its highest possible value. The strongest asset of our approach, though, consists of the simultaneous use of deterministic and probabilistic methods. The deterministic method produces concrete values that can be referenced against specific ICER thresholds, even though there is much debate around the way willingness-to-pay thresholds are established and used [[49]]. The probabilistic method encompasses diverse scenarios for costs and outcomes valid in both resource-abundant and resource-constrained health systems and provides a wide perspective on the economic implications determined by Cerebrolysin usage.

The emergence of health systems from the pandemic paradigm surfaces an imperative for more consistent use of economic evidence in healthcare decision-making and resource allocation. As the burden of stroke is estimated to increase in the following decades [[50]], strategies for stroke care need to be carefully crafted and regularly revised so that they strike a balance between producing health gains and remaining sustainable. Such an approach requires perpetual assessment of the cost-effectiveness of both existing and emergent therapies for stroke based on newly formed evidence on costs and outcomes.

Our results indicate a favorable cost-effectiveness profile for Cerebrolysin add-on treatment in moderate–severe acute ischemic stroke based on the CARS treatment paradigm at a 50,000 EUR cost-effectiveness threshold. Cost-effectiveness thresholds are used to determine whether an intervention is considered cost-effective in comparison to a relevant alternative, such as the standard of care. These thresholds typically represent the maximum amount a decision-maker, such as a healthcare payer, is willing to pay for an additional unit of health outcome, such as a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). It is important to note that there is no universally agreed-upon threshold, as the appropriate value depends on the specific context, including the health care system, the country’s willingness to pay and the disease area being studied.

In our sensitivity analysis, we chose a 50,000 EUR threshold as the maximum threshold in line with the definition of high-value interventions from the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review’s Value Assessment Framework [[51]]. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that different stakeholders may have different thresholds based on their priorities and resources. To account for this variability, we used cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) to explore the likelihood of Cerebrolysin being cost-effective across a range of potential threshold values. CEACs help decision-makers understand the probability of an intervention being cost-effective at different willingness-to-pay thresholds, allowing for a more flexible and context-specific interpretation of the results. This approach helps convey the uncertainty in our analysis and allows stakeholders to make informed decisions based on their unique circumstances and priorities. Our result must be interpreted against the objectives of health systems. Despite several attempts to reform Health Technology Assessment [[52]], Romania still uses a scorecard system based on assessments from other countries [[53]]. Therefore, a cost-effectiveness threshold has not been set by the public payer. While previous works from the World Health Organization (WHO-CHOICE) have suggested such thresholds may be set in line with per capita gross domestic product, there is wide criticism of such recommendations as they have no link with willingness to pay [[54]]. While priorities in the Romanian health system and the population’s health-related preferences are a rich ground for debate, we argue the threshold itself if not relevant in the context of this trial-based cost-effectiveness analysis, as QALY gain is underestimated over the chronic phase of stroke that follows after the initial 90 days of treatment. The question whether Cerebrolysin would be cost-effective in Romania under the CARS protocol remains difficult to answer in the absence of a decision-analytic model that accounts for a longer post-stroke timespan. Nevertheless, this analysis paves the way for future economic evaluations of this agent performed in different contexts, countries and from various other perspectives. It simultaneously adds to the evidence base to be used for shaping future strategies aimed at effectively and sustainably reducing the currently heavy societal burden of stroke.

headline.evidence: Table 1, Standard Treatment column: Sample size 93; Mean 1050 EUR; Median 1767 EUR; Lower threshold (95%) 1029 EUR; Upper threshold (95%) 1070 EUR; Standard deviation 101 EUR. A median of 1767 requires at least half the 93 patients to sit at or above 7.10 standard deviations above the mean; Cantelli's inequality caps that share at 0.0195, so the distribution-free admissible range for the proportion below 1767 is [0.9805, 1.0000] against the 0.5 a median asserts.
headline.plain: The paper says the typical (middle) placebo patient cost 1767 euros, but also says the average was 1050 euros and that costs barely varied around that average. Those two statements cannot both be true of the same 93 patients, no matter how the costs were spread out. The most likely explanation is a typing slip in one number rather than a problem with the analysis, because every other figure in that column fits together.

findings.reported: Sample size 93; Mean 1050 EUR; Median 1767 EUR; Standard deviation 101 EUR; 95% bounds 1029-1070 EUR.
findings.computed: Distribution-free violation confirmed on re-run: the proportion of the sample below 1767 EUR is bounded by Cantelli's inequality to [0.9805, 1.0000], while a median asserts 0.5000 (46/93). The reported proportion's own 95% interval [0.3893, 0.6003] lies entirely outside the admissible range. z = 7.10; two-sided binomial p = 0. The tool's explanation states the inconsistency holds 'with no distributional assumption at all'. The identical check on the Cerebrolysin arm (mean 1458, SD 106, n 100, median 1466) returns consistent (p = 0.55, no distribution-free violation), confirming the method is not simply rejecting skewed cost data.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values. The verdict does NOT rest on assuming cost data are normally distributed -- the distribution-free (Cantelli) bound is what is violated, and it holds for any distribution whatsoever. Values were re-read from the XML table grid at source; the table carries alignment_uncertain: false, image_only: false, and no merged body cells.

consequence.explanation: This corrects the sweep's reading: the paper's three incremental cost-effectiveness ratios are built from the difference in MEAN costs (1458 - 1050 = 408 EUR, which reconciles exactly), not from medians, so the anomalous median changes no reported ICER -- it damages confidence in the cost dataset and in the descriptive characterisation of placebo costs, without flipping any result the paper concludes from.

findings.plain: For the 93 patients who got standard care, the paper reports an average cost of 1050 euros, says costs clustered tightly around that average, and then reports the middle patient cost 1767 euros. A middle value that high would require half the patients to be extraordinarily expensive, which contradicts the tight clustering. The same check on the other treatment group passes cleanly, so this is one specific number that does not fit, not a flaw in how the check was applied. Importantly, the paper's headline cost-effectiveness figures are calculated from averages, not from this middle value, so no headline conclusion changes -- but the raw patient costs are published, and the authors could settle this immediately.

findings.title: Ordinal and standard-gamble ICERs ordered against their own QALY increments in Table 2
findings.location: Table 2 (QALYs Derived from CARS columns against Deterministic ICER column); Methods 2.3; Results paragraph 3
findings.reported: Table 2: Bayesian posterior 0.166 vs 0.156, ICER EUR 26,981; Ordinal 0.182 vs 0.168, ICER EUR 18,788; Standard gamble 0.186 vs 0.171, ICER EUR 20,618. Results text: 'The lowest ICER values were determined based on the ordinal valuation (18,788 EUR/QALY)'.
findings.computed: Summation checks confirm the three printed QALY increments are exactly 0.010 (Bayesian), 0.014 (ordinal) and 0.015 (standard gamble), and that the incremental cost reconciles exactly (1050 + 408 = 1458 EUR; 5197 + 2017 = 7214 RON). The paper's own formula (Methods 2.3) has a numerator -- incremental cost -- that does not depend on the valuation model, so ICER must be strictly decreasing in the QALY increment. The required order is therefore Bayesian > ordinal > standard gamble. The printed order is Bayesian (26,981) > standard gamble (20,618) > ordinal (18,788): the ordinal and standard-gamble rows are inverted. No division was performed; the finding rests on the tool-verified increments plus the ordering of printed values.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the incremental cost numerator is common to all three ICERs, which the paper's stated formula requires (cost terms carry no valuation-model dependence) and which the 408 EUR figure in Results asserts. Caveat stated explicitly: the QALY columns are printed to three decimals, so the unrounded increments have overlapping rounding intervals and the inversion is an inconsistency between the printed table and the printed ICERs rather than a strict impossibility. No tool in this kit computes or verifies an ICER, so the three values themselves remain unreproduced.

consequence.explanation: The Results sentence naming ordinal valuation as producing the lowest ICER, and the abstract's cost-effectiveness range that is anchored on it, both depend on an ordering that Table 2's own QALY columns contradict.

findings.plain: The paper's headline number is a cost per unit of health gained: extra cost divided by extra health. The extra cost is the same in all three of the paper's calculations, so whichever method found the most health gain must show the lowest cost per unit. The table shows one method finding less health gain than another, yet reporting a lower cost per unit -- which is backwards. The paper then singles out that method in its results text as the best-value one. Either the printed health gains or the printed cost-per-unit figures are wrong; from the article alone a reader cannot tell which.

findings.title: Probabilistic sensitivity analysis bounds QALY uncertainty by between-model spread rather than sampling variability
findings.location: Methods 2.4, Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis; supports the abstract's headline 80% claim
findings.reported: 'PSA random sampling was performed based on log normal (QALYs) or uniform (costs) distributions. The highest and lowest aggregate values by health state valuation model were used as the upper and lower bounds of QALY distributions for patient groups.'
findings.computed: Not a numerical recomputation -- a design-validity reading of the stated method. The bounds of the QALY uncertainty distribution are taken from the spread across the three valuation models (the three aggregate values per arm in Table 2), which is structural uncertainty about how to score a fixed set of patients. It is a different quantity from the sampling uncertainty in the mean QALY, which depends on between-patient variance and n and is nowhere reported: Table 2 gives no standard deviation, standard error or interval for any QALY value. Substituting the former for the latter would generally understate the uncertainty in the incremental QALY, because between-patient variance is excluded entirely. Costs are additionally sampled from a uniform distribution, an unusual choice for skewed cost data, and its bounds are not stated.
findings.assumptions: Rests on the Methods text as written; if the authors in fact sampled patient-level QALYs and used the model range only to set support limits, the concern is reduced. No dispersion statistic for QALYs is published anywhere in the paper, so the magnitude of any understatement cannot be quantified from the article.

consequence.explanation: The abstract's and conclusion's central claim -- an 80% probability of cost-effectiveness at 50,000 EUR per QALY -- is read directly off this simulation, so the width of the input distribution determines it.

findings.plain: The paper's headline claim is that there is an 80% chance the treatment is good value. That percentage comes from a simulation, and a simulation is only as honest as the range of uncertainty fed into it. The authors appear to have set that range using the difference between three ways of scoring the same patients, rather than the natural variation between the patients themselves. Those are different things, and the substitution would tend to make the result look more certain than the data support. The paper publishes no measure of how much patients varied, so a reader cannot check how much this matters.

findings.title: QALY horizon described as both the first year after stroke and 90 days
findings.location: Methods 2.1 and Discussion paragraph 4, against Table 2 caption, Methods 2.1 formula, and Results/Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis
findings.reported: Methods 2.1: 'The utility scores generated were used to calculate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) for the first year after stroke onset.' Discussion: 'the first explicit measure of change in QALY values between standard therapy and Cerebrolysin add-on scheme for ischemic stroke in the first year after the event.' Against Table 2 caption: 'Mean QALYs derived from CARS SF-36 data for 90 days after stroke'; and Results: 'considering only the 90-day timeframe of the CARS-study.'
findings.computed: No recomputation required -- the paper's own stated formula settles it. The QALY formula '(2*D2 + 88*AVERAGE(D2,D90))/90 * 0.25' averages utility over 90 days and multiplies by 0.25, i.e. a quarter of a year, which is the 90-day horizon and not the first year. Two passages therefore describe the horizon as four times longer than the formula, the table caption and the results text all state.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements; the formula is quoted verbatim from Methods 2.1.

consequence.explanation: A cost per QALY is uninterpretable without its time horizon, and the Discussion's novelty claim -- the first measure of QALY change in the first year after stroke -- describes a horizon four times longer than the analysis actually covers.

findings.plain: A 'cost per year of good health gained' figure means nothing unless you know what period it covers. The methods section says the health gains were calculated for the first year after stroke, but the formula printed just below it, the table heading, and the results section all say 90 days. The paper's claim to be the first study measuring this over a full year therefore overstates what it did by a factor of four.

findings.title: Headline QALY gain stated as 0.051 in the Discussion and as 0.01-0.015 in the Results
findings.location: Results paragraph 2 and Discussion paragraph 4, against Table 2
findings.reported: Results: 'a mean increment in QALYs between 0.01-0.015, depending on the valuation technique (Table 2)'. Discussion: 'Aggregated QALYs for the Cerebrolysin group were higher than those for the placebo group (0.051 average difference across the three health state valuation models)'.
findings.computed: 0.051 lies outside the interval [0.01, 0.015] the paper itself states -- a containment check, no arithmetic required. Summation checks confirm the Results range correctly describes Table 2: the Bayesian increment is exactly 0.010 and the standard-gamble increment exactly 0.015. The underlying cause is a scale confusion: the Results also print 'QALYs ... aggregated by health state valuation model: standard gamble (0.698 Cerebrolysin vs. 0.643 placebo), ordinal (0.704 vs. 0.647) and Bayesian posterior mean (0.653 vs. 0.613)', values roughly four times Table 2's in the same rank order. Those are SF-6D utilities, not QALYs -- the stated formula multiplies utilities by 0.25 -- so the narrative appears to have been carried forward on the utility scale while the tables report the QALY scale.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values; the identification of the text values as utilities rather than QALYs follows from the paper's own formula and is offered as the explanation, not as an additional charge.

consequence.explanation: The size of the health benefit -- the denominator of every cost-effectiveness ratio in the paper -- is stated at two values differing more than threefold, and the Discussion's benefit claim rests on the larger one.

findings.plain: The paper states how much extra health the treatment delivers in two places, and the two figures differ by more than three times. Two different sets of numbers also appear under the same label of 'QALYs' -- one set in the text, a set roughly four times smaller in the table. The likeliest explanation is that the written discussion used raw quality-of-life scores while the tables used those scores converted into the study's actual health-gain units. It is a labelling failure rather than a computational one, but it means the paper's stated benefit depends on which paragraph you read.

findings.title: Baseline comparability of the 193-patient subsample asserted with no table, statistic or p-value
findings.reported: 'We compared baseline characteristics (demographics, stroke severity, social and medical history) of the 193 patients for whom we calculated QALYs. No major differences were found, allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups.'
findings.computed: statcheck recovered zero NHST statistics from the entire body text. The paper presents no baseline table, no test statistics, no p-values and no confidence intervals for this comparison, so the Carlisle/Stouffer baseline-similarity test and the Table-1 dispersion check have nothing to operate on and absence_of_evidence cannot run. The claim is unverifiable as published. Note that this is a re-derived subsample: 15 of the 208 transferred patients were dropped for missing SF-36 data (10 for missing subscales, 5 by the converter), so baseline balance does not follow automatically from the parent CARS trial's randomisation and genuinely required demonstrating here.
findings.assumptions: The absence of inferential statistics is itself unremarkable in an economic evaluation and is not treated as a defect; what is reported here is that one specific comparative claim is made and left unsupported. No baseline-uniformity pattern could be evaluated in either direction -- there are no baseline p-values to be suspiciously high or suspiciously low.

consequence.explanation: The sentence 'allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups' is the stated licence for the entire arm-versus-arm comparison, and nothing in the paper substantiates it.

findings.plain: The authors dropped 15 of 208 patients because of missing questionnaire data, leaving a group that is no longer the one the original trial randomly assigned. They state that the two treatment groups still looked alike at the start, and use that to justify comparing them -- but they show no table and no supporting numbers at all. A reader has to take the claim on trust, and none of the standard checks for whether groups really were comparable can be run on what is published.

findings.title: Abstract's upper cost-effectiveness bound of 29.9 thousand EUR absent from the paper's own results
findings.location: Abstract, against Results paragraph 3 and Table 2 (Deterministic ICER column)
findings.reported: Abstract: 'Deterministic analysis based on sample mean values indicates Cerebrolysin would be cost-effective at a threshold between roughly 18.8 and 29.9 thousand EUR, depending on valuation techniques.' Table 2 ICERs: EUR 26,981, EUR 18,788, EUR 20,618. Results: 'the highest were concluded for the Bayesian posterior valuation method (26,981 EUR/QALY)'.
findings.computed: Textual comparison of printed values only, confirmed against the Table 2 grid re-read at source. The abstract's lower bound of 18.8 thousand matches Table 2's ordinal ICER of 18,788 EUR exactly, so the range is plainly intended to span the three tabulated ICERs; its upper bound of 29.9 thousand corresponds to no value anywhere in the paper, whose stated and tabulated maximum is 26,981 EUR/QALY.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values.

consequence.explanation: The abstract is the only part of the paper most readers see, and it overstates the upper end of the cost-effectiveness range by roughly 2,900 EUR per QALY relative to the paper's own maximum.

findings.plain: The summary at the top of the paper gives a range for how much the treatment costs per unit of health gained, topping out at about 29,900 euros. The paper's own results table tops out at 26,981 euros, and the figure of 29,900 appears nowhere else in the article. The bottom of the range matches the table exactly, so this looks like the top end was mistyped or carried over from an earlier version.

findings.title: Overstated claim that three valuation models rule out variation in patient preferences
findings.location: Discussion, paragraph 4 (health-state valuation passage); minor errors in Discussion paragraphs 5-6 and the same paragraph
findings.reported: 'Using all three valuation models and comparing their results can offer valuable insights into the robustness and sensitivity of the derived utility scores. By doing so, we can assert that there are no potential variations in preferences and risk attitudes which may impact the overall cost-effectiveness analysis.'
findings.computed: No recomputation -- a logical reading of a load-bearing sentence against the paper's own results. Applying three valuation models to the same fixed sample cannot establish that no variation in preferences exists; at most it shows the direction of the conclusion is stable across scoring methods. The paper's own three ICERs (18,788, 20,618 and 26,981 EUR/QALY) span a wide range that the abstract itself presents as its headline interval, which contradicts the sentence directly. The preceding sentence states the opposite intent, suggesting a drafting inversion rather than a substantive claim. Two typographical defects sit alongside it and are noted only because they co-occur: 'we argue the threshold itself if not relevant' (for 'is not relevant'), and the 2022 incident-stroke count written 'n = 37.225', using a decimal point as a thousands separator in an otherwise English-convention paper, leaving the intended magnitude ambiguous as printed.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements.

consequence.explanation: The sentence claims the choice of scoring model does not matter, while the paper's own three results span roughly 8,200 EUR per QALY and the abstract reports that spread as its headline range.

findings.plain: The authors write that because they used three different ways of scoring quality of life, they can assert there are no variations in patient preferences that could affect the results. That does not follow -- and their own three results differ substantially from each other, which is the range their summary advertises. The sentence immediately before says the opposite, so this reads as a drafting error rather than a claim the authors would defend.

findings.title: Duplicated participant rows in the supplementary QALY worksheet
findings.location: Supplementary dataverse workbook, QALY worksheet (1,737 numeric cells); verified pair at rows 119-120, patient IDs P-2-29 and P-2-32
findings.reported: The workbook records, per patient, day-2 and day-90 SF-6D utilities and a derived QALY for each of three valuation models -- nine numeric columns.
findings.computed: Restricting the scan to the QALY worksheet alone (so the Cost sheet's arm-level constants cannot contribute) returns 49 duplicated row pairs, 1 repeated column sequence and 20 repeated high-precision values, with tool severity highly_suspicious. I am recording this as indeterminate, a further downgrade from the sweep's suspicious, and the reason is structural. All nine numeric columns are deterministic functions of just two underlying quantities: the patient's SF-6D health state at visit 2 and at visit 7. The three valuation models are three fixed mappings of the same SF-36 responses, and each QALY column is a fixed formula applied to the two utilities in its own pair. A full nine-column row match is therefore ONE coincidence -- two patients sharing a health state at both visits -- not nine independent agreements, and the 17-significant-figure agreement is a floating-point artifact of identical inputs through identical arithmetic, carrying no additional information. Rulebook rule 11 guards (b) transformation artifacts and (c) finite-support ties both apply, and the converter's discrete lookup makes ties common by construction (the sweep observed one utility value recurring 27 times in a single column).
findings.assumptions: Assumes the nine numeric columns are the three (day-2 utility, day-90 utility, derived QALY) triples that the verified row's structure and the paper's stated formula indicate; the workbook's column headers were not enumerated in this stage. Adjudicating whether the matched patients are genuinely distinct requires the underlying SF-36 item responses, which are not in the workbook. Only the rows 119-120 pair was verified cell by cell, by the sweep; the other 48 are asserted by the tool and unexamined, and I read only the summary block of the tool's 185,000-character output.

consequence.explanation: These columns do feed the Table 2 QALY means that form every ICER denominator, so the consequence would be material IF the duplication were spurious -- but on the structural reading above it is expected behaviour of a discrete utility converter and supports no conclusion about the paper.

findings.plain: The authors published their patient-level data, and an automated scan found 49 pairs of patients whose numbers are identical all the way across. That sounds alarming, but it is largely explained by how the data were made: every number in a patient's row is worked out automatically from their questionnaire answers at two visits, so two patients who reported the same health at both visits will match on every column by design. The apparent agreement to seventeen decimal places is a by-product of a computer doing the same sum twice, not independent evidence. Settling this properly needs the original questionnaire answers, which are not in the published file. On the evidence available this is not a mark against the paper.

findings.title: Conflicting national ischemic-stroke denominators behind the 8.5 million EUR budget-impact estimate
findings.location: Discussion, paragraphs 5 and 6 (Romanian stroke care statistics)
findings.reported: 'By 2022, 3242 patients received reperfusion treatment, accounting for 7.8% of all ischemic stroke patients.' And: 'based on incident strokes reported by the Romanian Society of Neurology in 2022 (n = 37.225), a gross assumption that around 80% of cases would fit the ischemic indication ... the estimated budget impact ... would be roughly 8.5 million EUR per year'.
findings.computed: Not adjudicated. Establishing whether the two statements genuinely conflict requires dividing 3242 by 0.078 and comparing the result against 80% of 37,225 -- arithmetic no validated tool in this kit performs, and which I have deliberately not carried out. Both statements are quoted so a reader can check them directly. The magnitude of 'n = 37.225' is itself ambiguous as printed, since the same paper uses the decimal point as a decimal separator elsewhere.
findings.assumptions: None; this is recorded as unresolved rather than as an inconsistency. These figures are contextual background and do not feed the ICER, though they do feed the budget-impact estimate, which is separately unverified.

consequence.explanation: The two statements appear to imply different national ischemic-stroke totals for 2022, which is the base the roughly 8.5 million EUR annual budget-impact figure is built on; whether they actually conflict was not determined.

findings.plain: In discussing what this treatment would cost Romania nationally, the paper gives two separate figures for how many people had this type of stroke in 2022, and they appear not to agree. One number is also printed in a way that makes it unclear whether it means 37 thousand or 37 point 2. This affects only the paper's rough national cost estimate, not its main result, and we did not settle whether the two figures genuinely conflict.

not_checked.location: Table 2, Deterministic ICER column (18,788 / 20,618 / 26,981 EUR per QALY)
not_checked.reason: No validated tool in this toolkit computes or verifies an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Reproducing these three values from the stated 408 EUR incremental cost and the Table 2 QALY increments requires division, which was not performed. This is the paper's primary outcome and remains the largest hole in this review; the ordering argument in finding 2 constrains the three values relative to one another but does not reproduce any of them.

not_checked.location: Figure 2 (cost-effectiveness plane) and Figure 3 (cost-effectiveness acceptability curve)
not_checked.reason: Both carry numeric content appearing nowhere in the text or tables -- the full cloud of 10,000 simulated cost/QALY pairs, and the entire acceptability curve from 0 to 50,000 EUR. Only the single value 'roughly 80% at 50,000 EUR' is stated numerically. Anything read off the plotted marks would be figure-pixel provenance and barred from the exact-arithmetic checks, so the probabilistic sensitivity analysis that supports the abstract's headline claim is essentially unverifiable from the published article. Neither caption states what any dispersion marking represents.

not_checked.location: Supplementary dataverse workbook, 'Cost' worksheet - per-patient cost values
not_checked.reason: The worksheet contains the individual patient costs that would settle the Table 1 median anomaly outright, but computing a median from 93 raw values is hand arithmetic with no validated tool, so it was not attempted. This is the single most valuable follow-up available, and the data are already public.

not_checked.reason: Only the pair at rows 119/120 (P-2-29, P-2-32) was verified against the raw grid, by the sweep. The remaining pairs are asserted by the tool and were not examined cell by cell. Only the summary block of the tool's 185,000-character output was read in this stage; the per-value detail was not.

not_checked.reason: Verifying a currency conversion requires division and no validated tool covers it. Flagged for a reader because the two figures appear to round in different directions at the same stated rate.

not_checked.location: Methods 2.2 - reconciliation of the stated Cerebrolysin unit costs with the 408 EUR incremental cost
not_checked.reason: The paper states the components (three 10 mL vials at 5.5 EUR plus 0.6 EUR saline per day, over a 21-day course, plus 150 RON/day for acute discharges below 21 days and a 3% annual discount) but never shows how they combine into the 408 EUR increment. Reproducing this requires multiplication and division that no validated tool in this kit performs.

not_checked.location: Discussion, paragraph 6 - budget impact 'roughly 8.5 million EUR per year'
not_checked.reason: A product of a national incident count, two assumed proportions (80% ischemic, two-thirds moderate-severe) and a unit cost. No validated tool multiplies counts by unit costs.

The JATS body text extracted for this review did not include the article's back matter, so the funding source, competing-interest declarations and the formal data-availability statement were not read. This matters for a secondary analysis of a manufacturer-relevant product conducted by authors overlapping the parent trial, and a reader should consult those statements in the published article directly.

not_checked.location: Table 1 and Table 2 - automated per-cell sweep
not_checked.reason: 0 of 21 per-cell checks ran. Both tables are transposed relative to the usual layout, with each statistic occupying its own row rather than being packed into a 'mean (SD)' cell, so no cell carries an estimate together with its dispersion and the per-cell dispatcher had nothing to bind. The statistics were instead reassembled across rows by hand into check_estimate_ci and check_proportion_from_normal calls, which is what produced the headline finding. This is a limitation of the table shape, not evidence about the paper.

not_checked.location: Whole paper - baseline similarity (Carlisle/Stouffer) and Table-1 dispersion tests
not_checked.reason: Both require baseline p-values or per-arm baseline means/SDs, and the paper publishes no baseline table at all. The checks were considered and could not be run in either direction: there is no uniformity pattern here to flag or to clear.

not_checked.location: Whole paper - a-priori power analysis and multiple-comparisons correction
not_checked.reason: Neither applies. This is a secondary cost-utility analysis of a fixed existing sample with no hypothesis tests; statcheck recovered zero NHST statistics, so there is no family of p-values to correct and no power calculation to verify. Their absence is not a reporting defect here.

The headline quantity is a cost-effectiveness ratio, not a standardised effect size, and no dispersion is reported for the QALY difference, so no Cohen's d can be formed and no field benchmark applies.

limitations: FIGURES: this agent reads text and tables and did not view figure images in this editorial stage. The sweep located and cropped the three figures and read their captions at high crop confidence, but read no values off the plotted marks. Figures 2 and 3 hold the entire probabilistic sensitivity analysis -- 10,000 simulated cost/QALY pairs and the full acceptability curve -- and contributed nothing numeric to this review, so the paper's headline 80% claim rests on evidence that was not checked.

No GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT or SPRITE finding arose in this paper, so no R cross-check was applicable. The headline finding rests on Cantelli's inequality as implemented in check_proportion_from_normal, for which this toolkit offers no second engine; it was re-run once in this stage on inputs re-read from the XML table grid, and the paired control on the other treatment arm returned consistent.

This system reads ONE paper and reaches no network. Two questions that a duplication or data-integrity finding should be read against are outside its reach entirely: whether similar patterns appear in other papers by the same authors, and what the equivalent values look like in comparable cost-utility analyses of stroke therapies. The interpretation a reader needs is therefore partly ours and partly theirs.

No tool in this toolkit computes or verifies an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, which is this paper's primary outcome. The ordering argument constrains the three ICERs relative to one another but reproduces none of them, and the arithmetic that would reproduce them was deliberately not performed by hand.

The duplication tool's output for the QALY worksheet ran to 185,000 characters across 8,952 lines; only the first 70 lines -- the severity, the aggregate counts and the first duplicate group -- were read. The remainder of the per-value detail was not read, and that finding's downgrade rests on the structural argument about column dependence rather than on inspection of the individual matches.

The article's back matter (funding, competing interests, formal data-availability statement) was not present in the extracted body text and was not read. No inference about author independence or sponsorship is drawn anywhere in this review.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1 reports, for the 93 standard-treatment patients, a mean total medical cost of 1050 EUR, a standard deviation of 101 EUR, 95% bounds of 1029-1070 EUR, and a median of 1767 EUR. The mean, SD and bounds are mutually consistent, but a median of 1767 would require at least half the sample to lie more than seven standard deviations above the mean. Could you confirm the median for that arm, computed from the per-patient values in the Cost worksheet of your Dataverse deposit?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles the headline finding outright from data the authors have already published, and distinguishes a transcription slip from a problem in the cost dataset.

questions_for_authors.question: Your ICER formula uses a single incremental cost numerator (408 EUR) for all three valuation models. Table 2 shows a smaller Cerebrolysin-minus-placebo QALY increment for the ordinal model (0.182 vs 0.168) than for standard gamble (0.186 vs 0.171), yet reports the ordinal ICER as lower (18,788 vs 20,618 EUR/QALY). Could you supply the unrounded QALY increments and the incremental cost used for each of the three ICERs?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the inversion is an artifact of rounding the QALY columns to three decimals or an error in the ICER column, and would allow the paper's primary outcome to be reproduced.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state a mean QALY increment of 0.01-0.015 depending on valuation technique, while the Discussion states a 0.051 average difference across the three models. The Results also report values of 0.698 vs 0.643, 0.704 vs 0.647 and 0.653 vs 0.613 labelled as QALYs, roughly four times the corresponding Table 2 values. Could you clarify which of these figures are SF-6D utilities and which are QALYs?
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves a threefold discrepancy in the paper's headline benefit estimate and identifies which scale each reported set belongs to.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods 2.4 states that 'the highest and lowest aggregate values by health state valuation model were used as the upper and lower bounds of QALY distributions for patient groups'. Could you confirm whether the QALY uncertainty in the 10,000-iteration simulation was derived from the spread across the three valuation models, or from between-patient sampling variability, and provide the standard deviation of the per-patient QALYs in each arm?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the 80% probability of cost-effectiveness reflects sampling uncertainty in the incremental QALY; the paper reports no dispersion for any QALY value.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods 2.1 states that QALYs were calculated 'for the first year after stroke onset' and the Discussion describes the result as the first measure of QALY change 'in the first year after the event', while the QALY formula multiplies by 0.25, Table 2's caption specifies 90 days, and the Results specify the 90-day CARS timeframe. Which horizon do the reported QALYs and ICERs cover?
questions_for_authors.why: A cost per QALY cannot be interpreted without its time horizon, and the two descriptions differ by a factor of four.

This is a secondary cost-utility analysis. The authors obtained individual patient data from the 2016 CARS randomised trial of Cerebrolysin in moderate-severe acute ischemic stroke, mapped SF-36 responses onto SF-6D health utilities using the Sheffield converter, derived quality-adjusted life years over a 90-day horizon, attached actual Romanian hospital reimbursement costs, and computed three incremental cost-effectiveness ratios -- one for each of three health-state valuation models. They conclude that Cerebrolysin is cost-effective, with an 80% probability at a willingness-to-pay threshold of 50,000 EUR per QALY.

## What verifies

A substantial amount, and it is worth stating before the problems. The participant flow reconciles exactly at every step: 208 records transferred, 10 excluded for missing SF-36 subscales, 5 dropped by the converter, 193 analysed, 100 plus 93 by arm. The cost arithmetic reconciles in both currencies. Within Table 1, the means, standard deviations and 95% bounds cohere in both arms -- the interval half-widths recover a standard error of 10.46 in each case, which is what the printed SDs over the printed sample sizes imply. All three QALY increments in Table 2 reconcile with the QALY columns printed beside them. Sample sizes show ordinary non-round variation. Every check that could be run on the descriptive tables passed except one, which is what a carefully assembled table looks like, and it is precisely that coherence that isolates the single dissenting cell.

The paper also deposited its participant-level workbook publicly on Dataverse. That is the opposite of the state-but-withhold pattern, it is uncommon in this literature, and it is why several of the questions raised here can actually be settled by the authors rather than merely asked.

## Reading the median anomaly correctly

The sweep characterised the Table 1 median contradiction as reversing the direction of the paper's central cost comparison. That overstates it, and I have corrected the scope. The three ICERs are built from the difference in *mean* costs -- 1458 minus 1050, giving the 408 EUR increment, which reconciles exactly -- not from medians. The median is a descriptive statistic that no reported conclusion consumes. So the contradiction is exact, distribution-free, and rests entirely on the paper's own four printed numbers, but it flips nothing. What it does is put a question mark over the cost dataset at exactly the point where that dataset is least visible, and the benign reading -- a transcription slip, since every other value in that column fits -- is also the likeliest one.

## The primary outcome is the weakest-evidenced part

No tool here computes an ICER, so the paper's three headline values could not be reproduced. What can be established without division is their *ordering*, and it does not hold. With a numerator common to all three models, as the paper's own formula requires, the cost per QALY must fall as the QALY increment rises. Table 2's ordinal row shows a smaller increment than its standard-gamble row yet is printed with the lower ICER, and the Results text then singles that model out as producing the lowest values. The printed QALYs are rounded to three decimals, so their true increments have overlapping rounding intervals and this is an inconsistency rather than an impossibility -- but it means the paper's primary result cannot be checked against its own table.

The probabilistic analysis is weaker still. It appears to set the QALY uncertainty distribution from the spread across three ways of scoring a fixed sample, rather than from variation between patients. Those are different quantities, and substituting one for the other would generally make the 80% figure look firmer than the data warrant. No dispersion statistic for QALYs appears anywhere in the paper, so the size of that effect cannot be recovered from the article, and the simulation itself exists only as two figures.

## One defect with several symptoms

The horizon confusion, the two different value sets both labelled QALYs, and the threefold disagreement over the headline benefit are not three independent errors. They are one: the narrative was carried forward on the raw utility scale while the tables report the quarter-year QALY scale, and the horizon description drifted with it. That reading is supported by the paper's own formula, which multiplies utilities by 0.25.

## The raw-data signal, downgraded

I have moved the supplementary duplication finding down two bands, to indeterminate, and the reason is structural rather than charitable. All nine numeric columns per patient are deterministic functions of just two quantities -- the SF-6D health state at each of two visits. Three fixed valuation mappings and three fixed QALY formulas generate the rest. A full nine-column match between two patients is therefore one coincidence, not nine, and the seventeen-significant-figure agreement is a floating-point artifact of identical inputs through identical arithmetic. With a discrete converter and 193 stroke patients, ties are expected. This supports no conclusion about the paper either way, and adjudicating it would need the SF-36 item responses, which were not deposited.

The internal arithmetic of this paper is mostly sound, but its primary result cannot be reconciled with the table it is drawn from, its headline benefit is stated at two incompatible values, and its central probability claim rests on a simulation that is not reproducible from what was published. I would not rely on the reported cost-effectiveness ratios without the authors' clarification.
